\[
\hat\mu = \arg\min_\mu \sum_{q \in W} \rho\!\left(\frac{I_q - \mu}{s}\right),
\qquad
\mu_{t+1} = \frac{\sum_q w(r_q)\, I_q}{\sum_q w(r_q)},\quad r_q = \frac{I_q - \mu_t}{s}
\]

The formula shows the default parameter values.

where

- \(\hat\mu\): The robust estimate at the pixel
- \(\rho\): The loss of the estimator
- \(w\): The weight of a window pixel
- \(s\): The scale
- \(W\): The window

An M-estimator picks the value mu that makes the sum of rho of the scaled residuals smallest. With rho the square, that is the mean. With rho the absolute value, it is the median. Huber's rho is a square near 0 and grows only linearly beyond k, so outliers pull less. Tukey's biweight stops growing beyond c, so far outliers stop pulling at all. Holland and Welsch solve this by iteratively reweighted least squares. Each step weighs every pixel by w = rho' (r) / r and takes the weighted mean. Huber's weight is min(1, k / |r|) with k = 1.345. Tukey's is (1 - (r / c)^2)^2 inside c = 4.685 and 0 outside. These are the usual constants for 95 percent efficiency at the normal distribution.
